content:
Although Apple has long touted privacy as a selling point for its hardware and services, I do wonder whether the company regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

A fairly limited feature that nonetheless seems to attract almost monthly new antitrust lawsuits or regulatory challenges. In the UK, a third lawsuit involving ATT has now been launched—and there's a particular twist this time…

The Personalised Advertising Debate

Personalised advertising has long been one of the tech industry's most controversial topics. Instead of seeing random ads for products that may or may not interest us, we see ads tailored to our interests—collected through the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, it's a win-win for everyone. Consumers see ads that may genuinely interest them; advertisers get better returns on their ad spend thanks to precise targeting; and free apps and websites that rely on ad revenue likewise earn more for the same reason.

Although the data used to deliver personalised advertising is collected anonymously, the practice has bred widespread public perception that it invades privacy. Even though Apple developed a specific technology to ensure this data is anonymised, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency was designed to address this by letting consumers decide whether their data could be used to serve personalised advertising. Developers wishing to collect such data must obtain the consumer's consent.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, the move has triggered a slew of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, centring largely on the fact that Apple's own apps do not ask for this consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are actually consistent: its own apps don't display the ATT prompt because they don't collect the data the prompt covers. Third-party apps that don't collect such data are likewise exempt from having to show the prompt.

The Latest UK Lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three claims brought before the UK's relevant antitrust body, the Competition Appeal Tribunal. It lost the first case—though it is currently appealing—and the second is still ongoing.

Reuters reported on the third lawsuit, filed today.

And There's a Particular Twist

The latest case has an intriguing twist: it was brought by Ann Pope, a former senior official at the very regulator handling the case.

Leading the lawsuit, Ann Pope is a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority. She said Apple's policies "have caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." In a statement, Pope said: "This action is essential to protect the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure the rules Apple implements are fair, and to compensate UK companies for the losses they have suffered."

At the time of writing, Apple had yet to respond. The company recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU after Germany's antitrust watchdog opened an investigation into them.
